title: Ancient DNA Links Ice Age Europeans Across the Continent
paragraphs: Few epochs feel as remote as the Ice Age, yet a study in Science Advances, led by the University of Vienna and signed by 37 authors, suggests that its inhabitants were rather more connected than long supposed. The work turns on the Gravettian culture, which stretched across Europe from roughly 34,000 to 25,000 years ago.

At its core lies the genome of a woman who lived some 30,000 years ago in Isturitz Cave, in France, the oldest genome-wide dataset from a modern human in southwestern Europe. Though her ancestry was chiefly western, it was threaded with central and eastern European strands, and modelling places the admixture between about 32,500 and 31,500 years ago. “Our results show that eastern and western European populations were not as genetically isolated as previously assumed,” said lead author Pere Gelabert.

The team also teased DNA out of sediment in a 22,000-year-old layer at El Mirón Cave, in northern Spain, where no human bones or teeth survive; the authors take this to bolster the notion of Iberia as a refuge through the harshest stretch of the glacial cold. Caveats abound, however: the central result hinges on a single individual, several readings are couched as probable rather than proven, and the press release names no funding. It is a tantalising glimpse rather than the final word.

questions.a: The mixing of genetic ancestry from different populations.

questions.q: What did the sediment DNA add to the story?
questions.a: It suggested western ancestry persisted in Iberia, a possible Ice Age refuge, without human remains.

questions.q: Why is the study called “a tantalising glimpse”?
questions.a: It is intriguing but rests on very limited evidence.
